screens.title: Introduction to Linux Troubleshooting Methodologies
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting Linux is best done like detective work: with a plan, careful evidence collection, and safe experiments. In this lesson you will learn a structured methodology you can apply every time something breaks. We start by defining the problem and gathering facts: when it started, who is affected, and what changed recently. Then you will learn where to look for evidence — traditional logs under /var/log and the systemd journal — and which command-line tools like dmesg and lsof reveal kernel messages and resource usage. You will practice isolating the issue so you can test a hypothesis without making risky changes in production. Finally, we’ll cover documenting your steps and backing up configuration files before edits. A concrete example you will follow later is diagnosing an Apache service that fails to start because of a malformed virtual host file. A common misconception is that running random commands will fix things; instead, a measured approach preserves data and speeds resolution. By the end you’ll have repeatable steps and a checklist you can use on real servers. Which part of your current workflow feels least structured right now?

screens.title: A systematic troubleshooting methodology
screens.narratorSegment: A systematic troubleshooting methodology gives you a predictable path from symptom to solution. Define the problem in specific terms: what fails, when it started, and what recent changes might be related. Gathering evidence comes next — collect logs, current service status, and the outputs of diagnostic commands so you can form a testable hypothesis. The hypothesis should be a focused claim such as "a configuration error prevents the service from binding to its port." Test the hypothesis with minimal, reversible changes or by reproducing the problem in a safe environment. If the test confirms the hypothesis, implement the fix and then monitor logs to verify the resolution. If it fails, revise your hypothesis and try a different, isolated test. A concrete example is diagnosing a web server that won't start: you record the failure time, check systemctl to confirm the service status, look for configuration parse errors in logs, and test by disabling a suspect virtual host file. A common misconception is believing the first apparent error is the root cause; often it's a side effect. Your key takeaway: follow steps that produce evidence and preserve the ability to roll back. What small, reversible test could you run first next time a service fails?

content.html:
Core Concept Methodology
A systematic troubleshooting methodology
Define, gather, hypothesize, test, implement, document.
Definition & Steps
1. Define the problem
Describe symptoms, scope, and timing to narrow the search space.
2. Gather evidence
Collect logs, service status, and command outputs with timestamps.
3. Hypothesize & test
Form a small, testable claim and try a reversible change to validate it.
4. Implement & document
Apply the fix, verify in logs, and record steps so others can follow them.
Concrete example
# symptom: apache fails to start sudo systemctl status apache2 # gather logs sudo journalctl -u apache2.service --since "5 minutes ago" -xe # test by disabling a site sudo a2dissite broken.conf sudo systemctl start apache2
Common misconception
Seeing a single error line does not guarantee it is the root cause. Always check sequence and related messages before applying broad fixes.
Key Takeaway

Use small, reversible tests and collect timestamped evidence to confirm root causes before making permanent changes.

screens.title: Gathering information: key questions and first commands
screens.narratorSegment: Gathering information is the first and most valuable stage of troubleshooting. Ask targeted questions: what exactly failed, when did it begin, which users or systems are affected, and what changed recently. Concrete facts help you choose the right tools to collect evidence. Start with basic status commands: check the service status with systemctl, confirm active network interfaces with ip addr, and quickly probe reachability with ping. Record the outputs and timestamps so you can correlate later with log entries. For example, if a user reports that a website became unreachable at 10:15, note that time, run systemctl status apache2 to see whether it failed at or before 10:15, and capture journalctl entries for that window. A common mistake is changing configuration immediately; this can remove the evidence you need. Instead, capture a set of baseline outputs, then create a hypothesis. Document the commands and outputs in a single place so you or another engineer can reproduce the sequence. What one command will you remember to run first the next time a service is reported down? Gathering information: key questions and first commands means collect initial status, timestamps, and network checks to form a focused hypothesis without altering the system.. In practical terms, who, what, when, where — capture facts before you change anything. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Gathering information
Key questions and first commands to capture the baseline.
Targeted questions
  • What failed and when did it start? Capture exact timestamps.
  • Who or what is affected: single user, group, or system-wide?
  • Were there recent updates, config edits, or system changes?
  • Can you reproduce the problem now or does it happen intermittently?
Initial commands (record outputs)
sudo systemctl status apache2 ip addr show ping -c 3 10.0.0.1 sudo journalctl --since "10 minutes ago" -xe
Concrete example
A user reports a website went down at 10:15. You run systemctl status and journalctl for that time window. If the journal shows the service crashed at 10:14, you now have evidence to link the user's report to the service event and can inspect configuration or recent deployments made minutes before.
Pro Tip

Always capture outputs into a single log file or ticket note so you can search them later and show exact timestamps to stakeholders.

screens.title: System logs and /var/log
screens.narratorSegment: Traditional system logs are primarily stored under /var/log and contain a wealth of information about what happened and when. Files like syslog or messages record general system activity, auth. log tracks authentication events, and kern. log contains kernel messages. Applications and services often place their own logs in subdirectories, for example /var/log/apache2 for Apache. Real investigation starts with identifying which logs are relevant to the symptom. Use tools like tail, less, and grep to inspect and search entries. For instance, tail -f /var/log/syslog is useful when reproducing an issue in real time so you can watch new entries appear as you test. A common mistake is ignoring timestamps or missing related entries in other logs; always correlate times across files. A practical habit is to capture a slice of relevant logs with exact time windows to send with an escalation. For example, if an authentication fails at 09:12, include auth. log entries from 09:00 to 09:15 in your notes. What log file would you check first for an SSH authentication failure? System logs and /var/log means /var/log contains specific files for system, auth, kernel, and app-level events; timestamps are the glue for correlation.. In practical terms, where to look: syslog, auth.log, kern.log, and application logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
System logs and /var/log
Identify relevant log files and extract the time window you need.
Common log files
  • syslog / messages — general system events and service messages.
  • auth.log — authentication attempts, sudo, and login events.
  • kern.log — kernel messages and driver warnings.
  • /var/log/ — service-specific logs such as apache2/error.log.
Quick commands
# follow syslog in real time
sudo tail -f /var/log/syslog
# search for errors near a timestamp
sudo grep "Sep 10 09:12" /var/log/auth.log
Concrete example
If a service reports a permission denied error at 14:05, extract a 5–10 minute window from auth.log and the service error log. Comparing timestamps can show whether a failed authentication preceded the service error or is unrelated.
Common mistake

Overlooking timestamps or only searching a single log file. Always check multiple logs and align time ranges.

screens.title: journalctl — querying the systemd journal
screens.narratorSegment: Modern systems running systemd use a centralized journal that collects messages from multiple sources. The journalctl command is the interface to that data and is one of the most powerful tools for targeted investigation. Use journalctl -u unit to restrict output to a specific service, for example journalctl -u sshd to inspect SSH activity. The -xe options add extra context and jump to the most recent entries, which is useful after a failed service start. You can also constrain by time with --since and --until to capture the exact window you need. A common workflow is to reproduce the failure, immediately run journalctl with the unit and recent time window, and save the output for analysis. For example, journalctl -u apache2. service --since "1 minute ago" -xe shows recent failure messages with explanatory text. A misconception is thinking journalctl duplicates /var/log; it consolidates many sources but may not include every legacy application file, so check both. Your takeaway: learn time and unit filters to zero in on the relevant entries quickly. How would you capture the last two minutes of logs for a failing service?

keyIdea.title: Journal querying
keyIdea.text: Use journalctl filters by unit and time to obtain precise, contextual log entries for services.

content.html:
Definition
journalctl — systemd journal queries
Filter by unit, time, and follow to capture targeted entries with context.
Common commands
# show recent logs with context
journalctl -u apache2.service -xe

# filter by time window
journalctl --since "5 minutes ago" --until "now"

# show logs for sshd for the last 5 minutes
journalctl -u sshd --since "5 minutes ago" -xe
Concrete example
After attempting to start a service and seeing a failure, run journalctl -u that-service -xe to get recent entries and any explanatory text that systemd provides. Save the output to a file if you plan to escalate.
Misconception

Believing journalctl replaces all traditional logs. It centralizes many messages, but some services still write separate files in /var/log.

screens.title: dmesg and kernel messages
screens.narratorSegment: dmesg prints kernel ring buffer messages and is invaluable for diagnosing hardware detection problems, driver failures, and boot-time panics. Kernel messages often appear before regular service logs and can show device initialization failures or module load errors that block higher-level services. Use dmesg when services fail due to hardware or when drivers report errors during boot. Because the ring buffer contains many messages, pipe dmesg into less or grep for keywords you expect. Remember that dmesg output reflects kernel time, which may differ from systemd journal timestamps unless converted. An example: if a new NIC fails to initialize and the network service does not start, dmesg may show a firmware error or missing driver. A common mistake is ignoring dmesg when debugging boot failures; many boot issues surface there first. Your practical habit: capture dmesg output immediately after a failure and include it with other logs when you escalate the issue. What kernel symptom would make you check dmesg first? dmesg and kernel messages means use dmesg to surface hardware and driver problems that often precede service failures.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
dmesg and kernel messages
Inspect the kernel ring buffer for hardware, driver, and boot-time errors.
Quick commands
# view kernel messages paged
sudo dmesg | less

# search for 'error' or 'fail'
sudo dmesg | grep -i error
Concrete example
If a newly attached disk is not visible to the OS and a storage service fails, dmesg may report SCSI or driver errors. That information points to firmware or driver fixes rather than application configuration changes.
Pro Tip

Capture dmesg output immediately after a failure; it can be overwritten by subsequent boot cycles or ring buffer wrap-around.

screens.title: lsof and finding processes holding resources
screens.narratorSegment: lsof lists open files and is especially useful for finding which process is using a network port or holding a file handle. Use lsof -i :port to show processes bound to that port, including the PID and command. For example, lsof -i :443 finds which process is listening on HTTPS, which helps when a web server fails to start due to a port conflict. Contrast lsof with netstat or ss: while ss and netstat list sockets, lsof directly links a socket to the process and often provides more actionable information. A common mistake is scanning processes with ps and guessing which one handles a port; ps does not show port associations. Use lsof when you need the PID to stop a conflicting process or investigate why a file is locked. Concrete example: if a second web server instance occupies port 80, lsof -i :80 shows the unexpected process; you can then stop it and start the intended service. Final reflection: how would you confirm that stopping a conflicting process is safe before killing it? lsof and finding processes holding resources means lsof maps ports and files to processes, making it the preferred tool for identifying conflicts and locks.. In practical terms, identify which process owns a port, file, or socket. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison
lsof — find processes using ports and files
Prefer lsof to directly link sockets and files to processes.
Commands
# show process using port 80
sudo lsof -i :80

# find which process has a file open
sudo lsof /var/www/html/index.html
Concrete example & contrast
If a web server fails to bind to port 80, lsof -i :80 will reveal the PID of the current listener. While ss or netstat shows sockets, lsof ties the socket to a process name and PID making remediation straightforward.
Common mistake

Using ps to search for port numbers is unreliable. Use lsof to directly find the owner of the port.

screens.title: Isolate the problem and reproduce it safely
screens.narratorSegment: Isolation is about narrowing the surface area of the problem so you can test hypotheses confidently. Begin by asking whether the issue is reproducible and who is affected. If it is reproducible, capture the exact steps to reproduce it in a test environment or on a single non-production host. Scope checks include whether the problem occurs for all users, a single user, one application, or the entire system. A practical checklist might be: confirm the service status, test network connectivity, examine firewall rules, and inspect application logs. keyIdea.text: Simulate a failure in a safe environment, collect journal and error logs, then revert changes after verification.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Investigating a failed Apache service
Reproduce the failure, capture the journal and traditional logs, then clean up.
Scenario commands (lab only)
# stop apache and clear for a clean run (lab only)
sudo systemctl stop apache2
sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=1s
sudo rm -f /var/log/apache2/error.log /var/log/apache2/access.log

# create a broken config and enable it
echo "<VirtualHost *:80>" | sudo tee /etc/apache2/sites-available/broken.conf
sudo a2ensite broken.conf
sudo systemctl start apache2

# inspect journal and traditional logs
journalctl -u apache2.service --since "1 minute ago" -xe
sudo tail /var/log/apache2/error.log

# cleanup
sudo a2dissite broken.conf
sudo rm /etc/apache2/sites-available/broken.conf
sudo systemctl start apache2
Safety and notes
Only vacuuming the journal and removing logs is acceptable in an isolated lab. In production, do not delete logs; instead capture and archive them. When enabling a config file for testing, keep a backup copy so you can revert changes quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
Troubleshooting Linux is best done like detective work: with a plan, careful evidence collection, and safe experiments. In this lesson you will learn a structured methodology you can apply every time something breaks. We start by defining the problem and gathering facts: when it started, who is affected, and what changed recently. Then you will learn where to look for evidence — traditional logs under /var/log and the systemd journal — and which command-line tools like dmesg and lsof reveal kernel messages and resource usage. You will practice isolating the issue so you can test a hypothesis without making risky changes in production. Finally, we’ll cover documenting your steps and backing up configuration files before edits. A concrete example you will follow later is diagnosing an Apache service that fails to start because of a malformed virtual host file. A common misconception is that running random commands will fix things; instead, a measured approach preserves data and speeds resolution. By the end you’ll have repeatable steps and a checklist you can use on real servers. Which part of your current workflow feels least structured right now?

These learning objectives define the practical skills you will build. First, you will learn to apply a systematic troubleshooting methodology that turns symptoms into reproducible tests and clear fixes. This helps you avoid guesswork and unnecessary changes. Second, you will identify and interpret system log files and journal entries, recognizing where kernel, authentication, and service messages appear and how timestamps show sequences of events. Third, you will use core command-line tools for initial investigation: the kernel buffer via dmesg, process and socket mapping via lsof, and targeted journal queries with journalctl. Fourth, you will distinguish types of failures — application-level, kernel or hardware, and configuration problems — and match each to the right diagnostic steps. For each objective you will see a concrete example and a short verification task so that you can demonstrate competency. Throughout, you will be reminded to document steps and to back up configurations before making changes. Which objective feels most urgent for you to practice first?

These objectives expand the hands-on and safety aspects of troubleshooting. First, you will learn to gather full context: timestamps, recent changes, and whether the problem is reproducible by one user or system-wide. A concrete verification step is to reproduce a service failure and capture logs while doing so. Second, you will practice correlating events across multiple logs and the systemd journal; for example, matching a kernel message in dmesg to a service crash in the journal. Third, you will adopt safe practices: back up configuration files, avoid destructive commands without understanding them, and test changes on staging when possible. Finally, you will capture your troubleshooting steps and outcomes in a short log so escalation is clear and repeatable. Each card includes a short mnemonic to help recall the step sequence and a milestone you can show to prove competency. Which safety habit will you adopt immediately when you return to your workstation?

A systematic troubleshooting methodology gives you a predictable path from symptom to solution. Define the problem in specific terms: what fails, when it started, and what recent changes might be related. Gathering evidence comes next — collect logs, current service status, and the outputs of diagnostic commands so you can form a testable hypothesis. The hypothesis should be a focused claim such as "a configuration error prevents the service from binding to its port." Test the hypothesis with minimal, reversible changes or by reproducing the problem in a safe environment. If the test confirms the hypothesis, implement the fix and then monitor logs to verify the resolution. If it fails, revise your hypothesis and try a different, isolated test. A concrete example is diagnosing a web server that won't start: you record the failure time, check systemctl to confirm the service status, look for configuration parse errors in logs, and test by disabling a suspect virtual host file. A common misconception is believing the first apparent error is the root cause; often it's a side effect. Your key takeaway: follow steps that produce evidence and preserve the ability to roll back. What small, reversible test could you run first next time a service fails?

Gathering information is the first and most valuable stage of troubleshooting. Ask targeted questions: what exactly failed, when did it begin, which users or systems are affected, and what changed recently. Concrete facts help you choose the right tools to collect evidence. Start with basic status commands: check the service status with systemctl, confirm active network interfaces with ip addr, and quickly probe reachability with ping. Record the outputs and timestamps so you can correlate later with log entries. For example, if a user reports that a website became unreachable at 10:15, note that time, run systemctl status apache2 to see whether it failed at or before 10:15, and capture journalctl entries for that window. A common mistake is changing configuration immediately; this can remove the evidence you need. Instead, capture a set of baseline outputs, then create a hypothesis. Document the commands and outputs in a single place so you or another engineer can reproduce the sequence. What one command will you remember to run first the next time a service is reported down? Gathering information: key questions and first commands means collect initial status, timestamps, and network checks to form a focused hypothesis without altering the system.. In practical terms, who, what, when, where — capture facts before you change anything. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Traditional system logs are primarily stored under /var/log and contain a wealth of information about what happened and when. Files like syslog or messages record general system activity, auth. log tracks authentication events, and kern. log contains kernel messages. Applications and services often place their own logs in subdirectories, for example /var/log/apache2 for Apache. Real investigation starts with identifying which logs are relevant to the symptom. Use tools like tail, less, and grep to inspect and search entries. For instance, tail -f /var/log/syslog is useful when reproducing an issue in real time so you can watch new entries appear as you test. A common mistake is ignoring timestamps or missing related entries in other logs; always correlate times across files. A practical habit is to capture a slice of relevant logs with exact time windows to send with an escalation. For example, if an authentication fails at 09:12, include auth. log entries from 09:00 to 09:15 in your notes. What log file would you check first for an SSH authentication failure? The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Modern systems running systemd use a centralized journal that collects messages from multiple sources. The journalctl command is the interface to that data and is one of the most powerful tools for targeted investigation. Use journalctl -u unit to restrict output to a specific service, for example journalctl -u sshd to inspect SSH activity. The -xe options add extra context and jump to the most recent entries, which is useful after a failed service start. You can also constrain by time with --since and --until to capture the exact window you need. A common workflow is to reproduce the failure, immediately run journalctl with the unit and recent time window, and save the output for analysis. For example, journalctl -u apache2. service --since "1 minute ago" -xe shows recent failure messages with explanatory text. A misconception is thinking journalctl duplicates /var/log; it consolidates many sources but may not include every legacy application file, so check both. Your takeaway: learn time and unit filters to zero in on the relevant entries quickly. How would you capture the last two minutes of logs for a failing service?

dmesg prints kernel ring buffer messages and is invaluable for diagnosing hardware detection problems, driver failures, and boot-time panics. Kernel messages often appear before regular service logs and can show device initialization failures or module load errors that block higher-level services.
